Are you hiring for a programme in the GCC next year? 

A few early decisions will save you months later.

If you hire only strategists, you might find that nobody can build the plan, nobody knows the regulators, and the contract won't let you swap out a weak hire.

Here are 5 things to check before you start.

  • Builders next to strategists. 
A plan is only useful if someone can build it: the product, the data, the systems.

If you bring builders in late, they spend weeks catching up on a plan they didn't shape. 

Put them on the team from day one.

  • Local depth. 
Make sure your hires know local rules and regulations; if they have to get up to speed on this, you've already lost time.

  • Easy to exit. 
Long contracts are hard to undo if the wrong person turns up.

Split the work into stages and ask suppliers for free swaps, so changing course costs little.

  • Handover in the plan. 
When the experts leave, someone has to run and maintain what they built. 

Make time for your own people to learn the work while the experts are still there.

  • AI checks. 
AI can hallucinate and so ask every supplier how they check claims before a CV reaches you.

Which role can't your programme fill?

—

I'm Michael Mudau, COO at Sharp Minds. I help GCC firms and government entities bring in vetted ex-consultants, with three profiles in 48 hours. 

Follow for more.

Using AI to write smart contracts? Treat the output as untrusted until it passes your own gates.

Two recent studies, a 2025 workshop paper from the University of Genoa and a 2026 preprint from Deakin University, found that AI-generated Solidity can compile and look complete while still carrying serious security flaws. Both conclude it needs human-led checks before deployment.

Five gates to run before an external audit:
1. Write the spec (what must always be true) before the prompt
2. Compile cleanly and run static analysis on every pull request
3. Test beyond the happy path: fuzz and invariant tests
4. Review line by line, and mark which parts were AI-generated
5. Hand auditors the spec, tests and triaged findings

Law and accounting are often named as the careers most at risk from AI. In one room in the South West, those were the firms still planning to hire juniors.

Taught by Humans and techSPARK uk brought together seven professional services firms as part of their AI Talent Pipeline South West research. Laura Gemmell's write-up found:

• All of them use AI across the whole firm, from Microsoft Copilot to legal tools such as Harvey and Legora.
• All of them plan to hire juniors in the next 12 months.
• Juniors and trainees are often the keenest users. Some longer-serving staff are more cautious.
• New roles are appearing: legal engineer, innovation paralegal, legal technologist. One legal engineer said her role didn't exist six months ago.

Seven firms is one room, not a survey. So we looked at the wider UK numbers:

• Law: training contracts at 109 leading law firms are down 1.7% for 2027, from 2,593 to 2,549. Legal Cheek, which tracks them, links most of the dip to firms taking on more solicitor apprentices.
• AI in law: 61% of UK lawyers were using generative AI at work in 2025, up from 46% in January that year. Just over half of them chose tools built for law.
• Accountancy: 68% of mid-tier firms expect AI to reduce demand for some early-career accountants, but 83% say that won't directly mean fewer roles overall. They expect graduate hiring to fall 40% and school-leaver hiring to rise 49%.
• AI in accountancy: 86% of those firms say their tech strategy explicitly includes AI.

So the junior roles are still there, but the way in is changing, and more of it runs through apprenticeships and school-leaver schemes. Laura makes a point students should hear too: young people are told law and accounting are most at risk, so some rule them out before they even apply.

Our take: if using AI well is now part of starting out, the question for a graduate is how to show it. "Confident with AI" is easy to write on a CV. But student-built project an employer can open, read and watch shows how you actually work, which is exactly what we're trying to Showcase.

AI attracts the capital. Can insurtechs prove their value?

AI-focused businesses received 99.1% of insurtech funding in Q2 2026 and 83.2% in Q3, according to Gallagher Re.

That concentration makes AI impossible to ignore. It also raises an important question for founders: how will your business stand out among companies making similar claims?

An insurance buyer needs to understand what changes after adopting your product.

Will their team make better decisions? Can they process more business? How difficult will implementation be? What will the product deliver that they cannot achieve through their existing technology or internal team?

Gallagher Re highlights this challenge as insurers and brokers develop their own AI capabilities.

For insurtechs, our view is that differentiation needs to run through the whole business.

Product teams need a detailed understanding of the customer’s workflow. Commercial teams need to explain value in terms the buyer can assess. Implementation teams need to deliver that value within the realities of an insurance organisation.

A gap between any of those functions can weaken an otherwise promising proposition.

This has direct implications for hiring.

Technical capability is essential. So is the ability to connect it to insurance problems, navigate customer organisations and support adoption after the contract is signed.

For some businesses, the missing hire may be a product leader with strong insurance knowledge. For others, it may be someone who can bring discipline to implementation or build a more repeatable commercial process.

The right answer depends on where customer value is getting lost.

At FinPro., we believe that is a useful starting point for any growth conversation: identify the gap between what the technology can do and what the customer actually experiences.

Then build the team to close it.

Where is the hardest part of proving AI’s value today: the product, the business case or implementation?

Next: what this looks like in established insurance markets.

The skills AI can't automate are now the hardest to hire for.
 
AI tools now write boilerplate code, draft test cases, summarise tickets and generate documentation in minutes. Routine, well-defined work is getting faster and cheaper.
 
What has not become easier is hiring for the work around it. The skills that remain human are the ones that are hardest to see on a resume, hardest to test in an interview and slowest to build.
 
Here are 6 of them, and why they are tough to hire for.
 
1. Problem framing
 The skill: turning a vague business need into a clear, solvable problem before a single line of code is written.
 The hiring challenge: it rarely appears as a keyword. It shows only when a candidate asks the right questions.
 
2. System design and architectural judgement
 The skill: making trade-offs between scalability, cost, security and maintainability.
 The hiring challenge: tools can generate a design, but only experience can say whether it will hold at scale.
 
3. Critical review of AI output
 The skill: spotting the subtle bug, the hallucinated function or the security gap in generated code and content.
 The hiring challenge: it needs depth in the fundamentals, so junior profiles with tool fluency alone often cannot do it.
 
4. Stakeholder communication
 The skill: translating technical risk into business language, and managing expectations with product, clients and leadership.
 The hiring challenge: it is judged by how someone talks, not by what is listed in the skills section.
 
5. Ownership and accountability
 The skill: taking responsibility for outcomes in production, not just for the ticket assigned.
 The hiring challenge: it only becomes visible under pressure, long after the offer is accepted.
 
6. Learning agility
 The skill: picking up a new tool, domain or framework quickly and applying it with judgement.
 The hiring challenge: certificates show what someone studied, not how fast they adapt.
 
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HIRING
 The situation many teams face: the job description lists ten tools, but the real need is judgement, ownership and communication. Interviews test syntax while projects fail on ambiguity.
 
What works better:
 - Scenario-based and work-sample assessments over trivia rounds
 - Structured behavioural interviews with a clear scorecard
 - Skills-based hiring that looks at demonstrated capability, not only job titles
 - Contract or contract-to-hire engagements to evaluate fit on real work
 - A talent pool built around these skills before the requirement becomes urgent

 AI is raising the baseline for tools. It is raising the premium for judgement. The most valuable hire is no longer the person who knows the most tools, but the one who knows what to do when the tool is wrong.

Your mindset is very, very important. But what you feed your mind is just as important.

Yesterday, I posted about the importance of being careful about what we feed our minds and the kind of things we listen to.

I also talked about how easy it is to start believing that something isn’t working simply because that’s all you keep hearing or reading about it.

And guess what? I got another contract offer on Upwork yesterday. 

It got me thinking about something.

Imagine constantly hearing things like Upwork is dead, Fiverr is dead, nobody is hiring, there is no money in this industry, and so on.

If that’s all you keep hearing, at some point, you’ll start believing it. You’ll even begin to approach opportunities with that same mindset.

But the truth is, people are still getting jobs on Upwork. People are still making money on Fiverr. People are getting clients through LinkedIn and other platforms.

Yes, things might be challenging, and getting clients might not be as easy as it used to be, but that doesn’t mean the opportunities are no longer there.

Sometimes, we need to stop focusing so much on what isn’t working for other people and start looking at what is working for those who are getting results.

Be careful what you feed your mind. It matters more than you think.

And please, don’t let someone else’s experience convince you that you can’t get the results you’re looking for.

We keep going! 🚀

Rates for routine execution have flattened, while scarce specialists in AI/ML, Cloud Security, and Platform command 26k-38k PLN B2B net - with top Staff and Principal engineers hitting 35k-48k+ PLN, driven in part by global remote contracts.

When budgets miss that divide, everyone pays the price:

-> CEOs sign off on generic averages, only to face sticker shock mid-quarter.
-> CTOs watch Tech Leads burn hours interviewing architects they can’t afford to close.
-> HR gets caught squaring B2B net expectations with employment contract brackets - and in our data, compensation mismatch accounted for 16.1% of declined Senior-level offers.

At itMatch, before launching a search, we calibrate the full financial picture: benchmarking the real value of B2B vs. employment contract packages - including RSUs or 50% KUP - against actual architectural ownership.

Leaders often ask whether the market slowdown should make Senior engineers cheaper, or worry that higher offers will disrupt internal pay bands. For more standard delivery roles, rates have cooled, but engineers with scarce skills and broad ownership still have access to strong international opportunities, including remote contracts, which continue to influence their expectations. 

The key is to separate standard delivery roles from scarce, high-impact profiles.

If you align the budget with the real talent tier upfront, you avoid spending weeks on processes that were unlikely to close in the first place, and you have a much better chance of hiring the people who can genuinely move the team forward.

Most hiring teams are still debating whether AI interviews work.
 
The harder question lands on 13 May 2027.
 
That’s when India’s DPDP Rules become fully enforceable — and hiring is quietly one of the most data-heavy functions in any company. Think about what a single application leaves behind now:
 
→ A video interview recording
 → Voice data and a transcript
 → An ID document for verification
 → Proctoring footage from an assessment
 → An AI-generated score, and the reasoning behind it
 
By that date you need encryption or masking, access controls, monitoring and log retention, a defined retention period, security terms written into every processor contract — and a detailed breach report to the Data Protection Board within 72 hours of detection.
 
Penalties run up to ₹250 crore for inadequate security safeguards and ₹200 crore for failing to report a breach.
 
Here’s the line I’d underline for every talent leader: outsourcing the process does not outsource the accountability. If a vendor loses candidate interview videos, it is still your breach to report.
 
Three questions worth answering before the deadline becomes a scramble:
 
What do we collect in a hiring process — and do we actually need all of it?
How long do we keep an interview recording, and who decided that number?
If a vendor lost that data tomorrow, could we file a complete report in 72 hours?
 
At futuremug, we’re treating this as our own homework before it becomes a client questionnaire — documenting exactly what our AI interviews and assessments collect, how long a recording lives, who can access it, and who reviews a flagged case. That last one matters: with 5,000+ expert interview panels, a human sits behind any judgement that affects someone’s career. Not just a model, and not just a log file.
 
Candidates hand over their face, their voice and their ID because they want a job. That is trust before it is data.
 
Eighteen months is enough time to get this right. It isn’t enough time to start late.

Laid Off in IT? Your Next Job Depends More on How You Think Than How Much You Know.

A layoff may take away your job. But the wrong thinking can take away your next opportunity.

In my view, surviving layoffs in IT is not merely about updating your résumé, applying to hundreds of jobs or collecting more certifications.

It's about activating seven dimensions of strategic thinking. Let me explain it for you folks!

1. Causal Thinking - Diagnose Before You React.
Was the layoff driven by cost optimization, automation, restructuring or declining business demand? Understand the market forces before deciding your next move. Don't automatically interpret a business decision as a personal failure.

2. First-Principles Thinking - Secure Your Fundamentals.
Before pursuing another ₹50 LPA job, calculate your financial runway, monthly commitments and minimum acceptable compensation. Financial clarity gives you negotiating power.

3. Interdisciplinary Thinking - Reinvent Your Value Proposition.
Don't restrict yourself to your previous job title. Combine your technology, domain, business and leadership experience to position yourself for roles that solve larger organizational problems.

4. Divergent Thinking - Create Multiple Career Pathways.
One résumé. One job portal. One target role. That's not a strategy! Explore adjacent roles, GCCs, consulting, contract engagements and alternative career pathways.

5. Spatial Thinking — Map the Opportunity Landscape.
Identify where demand exists across industries, geographies, companies and job functions. Focus your efforts where your capabilities intersect with actual hiring needs.

6. Exploratory Thinking - Experiment Before You Commit.
Instead of blindly pursuing certifications, test your market relevance through recruiter conversations, interviews, networking and small practical projects. Let market feedback guide your upskilling.

7. Epistemic Curiosity - Challenge Your Own Assumptions.
Are you genuinely unemployable, or is your positioning ineffective? Is AI eliminating your role, or changing its expectations? Distinguish facts from fears and assumptions.
The Bigger Leadership Lesson

A layoff is an event. Unemployment is a situation. Career stagnation is a risk. Your response determines how effectively you navigate all three.

The professionals who recover effectively are not necessarily those with the most certifications or longest experience.

They are often those who can diagnose reality, reposition their capabilities, explore alternatives and execute a disciplined job-search strategy.

Because after 15–20+ years in IT, your next career breakthrough may require a different way of thinking, not simply more years of experience.

What's the biggest challenge after an IT layoff - financial pressure, loss of confidence, skill relevance or finding the right opportunities?

What is a lawyer actually for when AI can review a draft in seconds? 🤔

I took this question home from my first Alliott Global Alliance® Worldwide Conference in Amsterdam, after a panel where Omar Odeh (MIO & Partners) argued that young lawyers could become redundant. And yet he is still hiring young colleagues.  😉

The session, with Nicholas Nicolaou, Marjon Lok (DVDW) and facilitators Tom Dunlap and Chris Jones, asked how firms can grow junior talent, how to price our work when it takes less time, and how to build trust among clients and staff along the way. My three takeaways:

1️⃣ AI can review a draft. So why do clients still come to us? Because we are part psychological support (“Can I sign this contract?”) and part insurance: someone who stands behind the advice. Best-paid therapist? 😄

2️⃣ The bottleneck is not the technology, it is us. Do lawyers actually want to work with AI, and who controls how it is used? Our clients have already moved on: they ask AI first, just as I do before I see a doctor. For many people, AI has replaced the search engine.

3️⃣ More and more clients say: “I’ll send you my draft, you review it, and we save time.” That changes our role. The lawyer becomes the person who spots the risks ahead and, even more importantly, makes them visible. 💡

Beyond the panels, this conference was about people:

🇨🇳 Special thanks to Peter Pang and Claire Sun  (IPO Pang, Shanghai) for sharing so much insider knowledge about Chinese business culture.

🙏 And thank you to everyone who welcomed the first-timers so warmly.

PROCUREMENT FROM ZERO – DAY 36
What Would You Do in Your First 30 Days as a Procurement Professional?

Starting a new procurement role is not  just about raising purchase orders or requesting quotations. It is about understanding how an organisation spends its money and where value can be created.

If I joined a procurement team tomorrow, these are five areas I would want to investigate:
1. Spend Analysis
Where is the organisation money going? Which categories account for the highest expenditure? Are there opportunities to reduce costs?

2. Supplier Performance
Are suppliers delivering on time? Are we experiencing recurring quality issues? Are suppliers meeting their contractual obligations?

3. Contract Compliance
Are departments purchasing through approved contracts, or are we losing money through off-contract spending?

4. Cost-Saving Opportunities
Are we buying at competitive prices? Could supplier consolidation, better negotiation or strategic sourcing deliver savings?

5. Procurement Data
Are we using AI,Excel, Power BI or ERP systems to identify spending trends, monitor KPIs and support better purchasing decisions?

Don’t just process purchase orders. Understand the money, the suppliers, the risks and the opportunities to create value.
A question for procurement professionals, hiring managers and recruiters:

What would you expect a procurement professional to achieve within their first 90 days in a new role?

Most law interns want to work in AI law.
Very few know the route.

It isn't one big jump. It's five steps.

Here's the route I'd map for any law intern today:

1. Build the legal base
→ Contract Act, IT Act 2000, DPDP Act 2023 and the DPDP Rules 2025
→ Read the Act section by section, not just summaries

2. Learn how the technology works (no coding needed)
→ How data moves: collection, storage, processors, cross-border transfer
→ How AI models are trained, and what bias, hallucination and model risk mean
→ Read one privacy policy and one AI vendor contract every week

3. Add one global framework
→ GDPR, still the reference point for global privacy work
→ The EU AI Act's risk categories
→ NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 for governance in practice

4. Pick one or two certifications, not six
→ DSCI Certified Privacy Professional (DCPP) for the Indian context
→ IAPP CIPP/E for GDPR, or CIPM for running a privacy programme
→ IAPP AIGP for AI governance
→ Check the current syllabus and fees on the official site before you pay for any course

5. Build work you can show
→ Intern with a firm's TMT or privacy team, a startup's legal team, or a privacy consultancy
→ Draft samples: a DPDP notice, a consent flow, a data processing agreement and an AI use policy (no client data)
→ Write about what you learn, here on LinkedIn

The career path:
Law intern → Associate in a tech or privacy practice, or privacy analyst → Privacy counsel → AI governance lead or tech lawyer

The DPDP Act's main obligations apply from 13 May 2027. Companies will need people who can read both the law and the system.

If you run a firm, this is also the profile worth hiring and training now.

The law tells you what is allowed.
Governance shows how you prove it.

🌍 Work Mode: Remote

•	Experience designing MCP actions, semantic layers, or AI integration frameworks.
Nice-to-Have Skills:
•	Azure Integration Services.
•	MCP, Microsoft Copilot, Lyzr, OpenAI, or similar AI platforms.
•	Enterprise integration and middleware architecture.
Ideal Candidate:
A self-driven consultant who can independently analyse requirements, identify the required Oracle HCM APIs, validate workflows in Postman, and implement reusable MCP-based integrations for AI-enabled enterprise solutions.
